It is, but the US military is poorly organized for asymmetric warfare overall. A half dozen aircraft carriers, squadrons of supersonic fighter jets, and a few divisions of tanks are great if you're in a massive set-piece war on the plains of Europe, but they don't do so well looking for a few dozen people hiding in the mountains or in a city. A platoon of US personnel stands out like a sore thumb, and that convoy crawling down the road is visible for miles and audible for nearly as far. Meanwhile, one dude strapped with plastic explosives with scrap metal stuck to it can still fuck up a dismounted patrol and that supply line of dudes making IEDs on demand is still churning out a product that's blowing up trucks frequently enough to keep their money coming in. Meanwhile, the guy they're all trying to find is walking around in the next town over because the local security forces tipped him off last week.
That is why the US has made major increases to the size of its special operations units, built littoral combat ships and thousands of drones over the last ten years.

This is the case with any well-trained and well-armed army, not just U.S. forces. The Soviets had the same problem during their War in Afghanistan in the 1980s (a war they lost) and the French in Indochina (same). The local force (the one that often uses guerrilla tactics) knows the terrain and culture, has a strong sense of loyalty to a cause (whether it's nationalism, independence, a political or religious ideology, or a mix of these), is cheap to arm and field, and is not afraid to lose troops.

Guerrilla tactics work well against well-equipped and trained foreign armies. Case in point: the Continental Army was aided significantly in its victory against the British Empire during the American Revolutionary War with such tactics. The only way to counter such tactics is via effective intelligence and with the support of a powerful local faction. Otherwise it becomes a quagmire that is expensive and tedious. In such situations, the home team need not win battles, but simply continue to attack until the foreign army tires and withdraws. This is how it is argued that the U.S. lost the Vietnam War.

It's amazing to me that tax reform isn't a more widespread issue. I'm sure many people here would advocate a progressive tax scheme rather than Paul's flat tax plan, but they overlook the fact that an incredibly complex tax code like ours has regressive effects: there are so many possible deductions and exclusions in the code that only those able to afford to hire accountants can truly take advantage of them. With tens of thousands of pages to muddle through, simply raising the overall rate on the highest earners will have little genuine effect.

Whether you agree or disagree with Paul's idea for a replacement, you should almost certainly agree that the current tax code should be heavily simplified.
